pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 20: There are no dropouts. There are only students whose school hasn't been built yet.*

The sun rose over Dimblewick to find the courtyard buried under a sea of lavender-scented socks and gold confetti. It looked less like a schoolyard and more like a cat had been wrestling with a laundry basket.

Principal Thistlewood stood before the Great Hall, wrapped in a thick wool blanket that had once been a classroom rug. He clutched a mug of tea with both hands, his moustache drooping so far it hung damp and defeated to his chin.

The whole school stood in the square. The Golden Circle was silent. Even the portraits in the windows leaned forward.

"I was wrong," the Principal said. His voice cracked, so he cleared his throat and tried again. "I was wrong about the hat. And about you, Marnie."

He pointed a trembling finger at the Founders' Fountain. There, Wilhelmina Humbleton stood bareheaded, save for the tall purple hat perched on her stone head. It was crooked. It was tilted to the left by exactly the width of a thumb.

"It is on the statue where it belongs," the Principal announced. "Slightly crooked, as it turns out it prefers."

Marnie blinked. She looked at the hat, then at the goose, who was asleep on a pile of socks with his purple ribbon tied neatly around his neck. She did not smile. She just nodded, once, and she was fairly sure her head tilted a little to the side.
pages.image: Principal Thistlewood in a large blanket holding tea, standing before a stone statue wearing a crooked purple hat, while Gerald with a silver ribbon sleeps on a pile of colorful socks in a sunny courtyard.

pages.text:
Cassius Pomeroy approached the Fountain, his golden hair flopped to one side where a single strand of confetti was stuck in his blazer pocket. He looked as though he had been in a storm and lost the map, which was a new kind of terrible for a boy who always knew where everything was.

"I am sorry," he said, and his voice was stiff, like a gate that needed oiling.

Marnie waited. She did not move.

"I am truly sorry," he said, and his eyes went wide with the specific panic of a student who has just realized the test was on a topic they skipped. He had never done this before. Being sorry, it seemed, was a very new and difficult spell.

"It's okay to be wrong, Cassius," Marnie said. She kept her voice low. "You'll get used to it."

Cassius swallowed. He pulled out his silver wand, his hands shaking enough to make it look like he was trying to catch a fly. He aimed it at a puddle on the flagstones and whispered, "Dry."

The puddle got wetter. A single, soggy lavender sock popped out of the water and landed squarely on his shiny black shoe.

Cassius stared at the sock. He picked it up and squeezed it, watching water drip onto his polish. He looked at Marnie, his lower lip trembling. He did not cry, but he came very, very close.
pages.image: Cassius Pomeroy with messy hair and a wet sock on his shoe, looking delighted, while Marnie with copper-red hair buns watches him with a warm smile near a stone fountain.

pages.text:
A letter arrived from the Ministry, thick and heavy, smelling strongly of official ink. The Principal read it aloud to the club, who were sitting on the fountain steps.

"Marnie is offered reinstatement," he announced. "Full honors. A new desk. A new cloak."

Marnie felt a warm glow in her chest, which was nice, but it felt small, like a thimble inside a teacup, and too small for a whole room.

"I'll come back," she said. "But only if the others come with me."

The Principal cleared his throat, stroking his moustache as he looked at Bunt, then at Lulu, and finally at Toby.

"Very well," he said, taking a deep breath. "We are opening a new Department. The Department of Wonky Magic."

Bunt blinked, pulling a biscuit from his pocket. "Assistant Professor of Sneezing?" he asked.

"Bunt as Assistant Professor of Sneezing," the Principal confirmed. "Lulu in charge of Applied Socks. Toby as Professor of Reversal. And Marnie... Head of Sideways Studies."

Toby adjusted his gold glasses, looking down at his list. He crossed out the word "failure" and wrote "tool" in its place.
pages.image: Principal Thistlewood in a purple robe gesturing toward four students: a tall troll with a biscuit, a girl in an orange hoodie with a sock, a boy with glasses, and Marnie with red hair buns, all sitting on stone steps.

pages.text:
The celebration in Dimblewick started with a bang, or rather, a very loud thump that made the teacups rattle in their saucers.

Gran Pennywhistle was dancing. She held a broom in one hand and a cup of tea in the other, spinning in circles until her lavender apron flapped like a nervous flag. The broom swept the floor with aggressive enthusiasm, knocking over a stack of mops that tumbled down the lane like clumsy dominoes.

Mrs. Humphreys stood by the bakery door, her hair piled high with flour that stuck to her eyebrows like snow. She was juggling three buns, which was impressive considering one of them immediately flew over the street and was caught by a child who took a warm, sticky bite before even looking up.

A banner hung above Crumb Lane, painted by Lulu in wobbly letters that said "WELCOME BACK." She had apologized to the wall twelve times while doing the job, treating the plaster with more care than she treated her own socks.

Gerald stood on the cobblestones. Today was an odd day, which meant he was a goose. He honked at the sky, puffing out his chest. He was free, and he was making a point of it at lunchtime, ignoring the fact that he had been a hat just yesterday.

Marnie watched them all. She felt light, like a balloon that had finally been let go of the string and was drifting toward the roof.
pages.image: Gran Pennywhistle in a lavender apron dancing with a broom, Mrs. Humphreys juggling buns, and Gerald with a purple ribbon standing proudly on cobblestones in a village street.

pages.text:
Evening settled over the Potting Shed, where the stove hummed a low, cozy tune and the air thickened with the scent of lavender and woodsmoke. Marnie opened the Handbook, picked up her pen, and wrote Rule 20 in ink. The letters were neat, and they were certain.

*There are no dropouts. There are only students whose school hasn't been built yet.*

She closed the book and looked around at her friends, who were busy in their own way. Toby was checking his list, Lulu was counting socks, Bunt was eating a biscuit, and Gerald was asleep on the windowsill, his beak tucked under his wing like a secret.

Then, there was a knock.

It was a small, nervous tap, tapping, tapping, like a finger trying to remember which side of the door it was on. Marnie opened the door.

In the doorway stood a boy. He was small, his wand was bent, and he looked like he had just lost a fight with a very opinionated tree.

"I heard you take people who can't," he whispered.

Marnie remembered the morning she had been expelled. Fourteen minutes past nine. A Tuesday. The cold. The shame.

She reached into her pocket and pulled out a biscuit.

"We take everyone," she said. "Come in."
pages.image: Marnie with copper-red hair buns holding a biscuit, smiling warmly at a small nervous boy with a bent wand standing in the doorway of a cozy shed with a stove and flowerpots, with Gerald nearby.
